meta.title: Buying Land in Venezuela: What to Check Beforehand
meta.h1: Buying Land in Venezuela: Urban, Rural or Ejido, and What to Check Before Paying
meta.description: What to check when buying land in Venezuela: registered document, boundaries and measurement, zoning, services, ejido and rural lands, and why you should see the land in person.
meta.answer: Before buying land in Venezuela confirm that the seller is the owner according to a registered document, that the actual measurements and boundaries match the document and the cadastre, that the municipal zoning allows what you want to build, and that there is access to water, electricity and a road. Distinguish between private urban land, ejido (municipal) land and rural land, because each has different rules. Visit the land in person with a surveyor if measurements matter.

sections.h2: The title: who really owns it
paras: Ask for a copy of the registered ownership document and have a lawyer study the legal chain and request a lien certification from the Registro Inmobiliario. In land transactions, problems such as uncompleted inheritances, sales of "bienhechurías" without a land title, and ejido lands offered as if they were private are common.
If someone sells you only the "bienhechurías" (the structures or plantings) and not the land, be clear about what you are buying: it is not the same as owning the land.

The document describes the land with measurements and boundaries. In reality they may not match: running fences, partial invasions or old imprecise descriptions. A topographic survey done by a professional tells you what is on the land and whether it matches the document and the municipal cadastral record.
steps: Compare the document with the land’s cadastral certificate.
Hire a topographic survey if the land is large or the measurements are critical for your project.
Walk the boundaries with the seller and, if possible, with the neighbors.
Verify that there are no occupants or third-party constructions.

sections.h2: Zoning and what you can build
paras: The alcaldía defines what can be built in each zone: residential or commercial use, maximum height, land coverage percentage and setbacks. Request the zoning certificate or urban variables before buying, especially if you plan to construct a building or a commercial space.
A cheap lot may not serve you if zoning does not allow your project.

bullets: Water: is there a water-supply connection, a well, or will you have to rely on cisterns?
Electricity: is there a nearby grid or will you need to run a line?
Access road: public, paved, passable in rain?
Sewers or need for a septic tank.
Risks: proximity to streams, steep slopes or flood-prone areas.
sections.tip: Visit the land after a heavy rain day. You will see if it floods, if the access becomes impassable, or if there are runoff issues.

paras: Agricultural-vocation lands have a special regime and the Instituto Nacional de Tierras (INTI) intervenes in their regulation. Before buying a farm or a rural lot, have a lawyer with agrarian experience review the property situation, because there are figures such as adjudication or permanence guarantee that do not equate to full private ownership.

sections.h2: If you plan to build: calculate the full project
paras: The land price is only the beginning. Before buying, request a preliminary estimate from an architect or engineer of what your project would cost on that specific land. A sloped lot, fill soil or distance from service networks can greatly increase construction costs.
steps: Check the urban variables at the alcaldía to know what you can build.
Request a soil study if the land is sloped or you have doubts about its firmness.
Find out how much it costs to bring water, electricity and sewers to the land.
Obtain the construction permit from the alcaldía before starting work.
Set aside a contingency for unforeseen issues: in construction, they almost always appear.

faq.q: How do I know if a land has an owner in Venezuela?
faq.a: Request the registered ownership document and verify the legal history and encumbrances in the Registro Inmobiliario. Also check the municipal cadastre.
Land owned by the municipality. Its use or acquisition follows municipal procedures, and the occupant does not always own the soil.

faq.q: Can a foreigner buy land in Venezuela?
faq.a: They can buy urban lands. For rural lands or border and coastal zones there are special regulations that should be reviewed with a lawyer.
The constructions or improvements made on a land. Buying bienhechurías is not the same as buying the land.
The municipal rules about what can be built on a land: use, height, occupancy percentage and setbacks. Check them before buying if you plan to build.

faq.q: Do I need a surveyor to buy land?
faq.a: It is not mandatory, but it is highly recommended if the land is large or measurements matter for your project. It tells you if the reality matches the document.
